modalities.name: Not the Child's Job
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who look after their own feelings, so you needn't.
modalities.whatItIs: Not the Child's Job is a new, untested variation on ideal parent imagery for people who learned early to look after a parent's moods. In scripted scenes, the imagined ideal parents have ordinary hard feelings of their own, such as tiredness, worry or sadness, and visibly take care of them as adults, so the child you picture is free to stay a child.
modalities.coreIdea: Care here runs in one direction only: the imagined child gives nothing back, soothes no one and is told plainly that grown-up feelings belong to the grown-ups. A child who never had to manage anyone else's feelings may form a kind of security in which closeness does not come with a job attached.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly sessions with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work, a short settling is followed by scenes in a fixed order: an imagined parent comes home tired and says 'I'm worn out, that's mine to sort, you go and play', a sad parent turns to the other parent or a friend for comfort, and the parents disagree and settle it between themselves while the child carries on drawing. After each scene you notice in the body any urge to step in and fix things, and what it is like to be let off that job, while the therapist keeps the scenes clearly imaginary and never treats them as a search for memories.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who were the family's helper or peacekeeper as children and still feel responsible for everyone's moods, and who want to work on this with a trained therapist.
modalities.cautions: Watching imagined parents cope can stir grief or anger about the parent you had to look after, so this belongs only with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma care, at your own pace. The scenes are imagination, never memories or evidence of what happened, and they are never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: Were you the kid who kept a parent's mood afloat? Not the Child's Job is an untested idea: with a trauma-trained therapist, you picture ideal parents who handle their own tiredness and worry, so the child can just play. Imagination, never memories.

modalities.name: Raised by a Village
modalities.tagline: Imagined care from a whole circle of kind grown-ups.
modalities.whatItIs: Raised by a Village is a new, untested idea that widens ideal parent imagery from two figures to a whole imagined circle of carers: grandparents, an aunt, an older cousin, a neighbor. A trauma-trained therapist guides scenes in which the imagined child is looked after by one caring adult after another, each with their own way of doing it.
modalities.coreIdea: Security might feel sturdier when it is spread across a web of many carers than when it rests on a single bond, so that when one imagined carer is busy or unwell, another is already there.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over the first sessions you and the therapist build a cast of four to six invented carers, each with a name, a manner and a usual place in the imagined child's week. Later sessions guide 20-minute scenes, such as a family meal or a day when a parent is ill, in which the child moves between carers and is never left without someone. You end each session by naming which carer felt closest that day.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with a sense that care could vanish if one person let them down, who are working on attachment with a trained therapist and find rich imagery easy.
modalities.cautions: Imagined family scenes can bring up painful comparisons with your real family, so this belongs with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work. The carers are invented, the scenes are not memories or evidence of anything, and they are never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: What if imagined care came from a whole circle, not just two parents? Raised by a Village is an untested idea: a trauma-trained therapist guides scenes of grandparents, aunts and neighbors who each care for the child you picture. Invented carers, not memories.

modalities.name: The Child's Conclusions
modalities.tagline: Spelling out what a well-loved child would come to believe.
modalities.whatItIs: The Child's Conclusions is an untested concept that adds a quiet, word-based step to ideal parent imagery. After each scripted scene of care, you answer the same few questions about what a child raised that way would come to expect of themselves and other people, and a trauma-trained therapist writes your answers down word for word.
modalities.coreIdea: Early care teaches a child lessons long before it has words for them, so stating those lessons plainly after each imagined scene might help a new inner model take clearer shape than the feeling alone would. The body stays still and the work stays in words, the reverse of letting feeling move out through dance.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session follows the same order: a few minutes of seated settling, a 15-minute scripted scene with the ideal parents, then three fixed questions asked slowly by the therapist with long silences between them: what does this child expect when it is upset, when it asks for something, and when it gets something wrong? You answer with eyes closed while the therapist writes your words down without comment, and over the weeks the answers are gathered into a short handbook in the imagined child's voice, which the therapist reads aloud to you in the final session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with attachment worries who think best in words and want imagery work to leave a clear, written thread from session to session.
modalities.cautions: Comparing the imagined child's beliefs with your own can sting or stir grief, so this is for work with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma care. The scenes are imagination, never memories or evidence of what happened, and they are not used to search for forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: An idea: picture ideal parents caring for the child you were, then answer three quiet questions about what a child loved like that would expect. The Child's Conclusions is untested and meant for work with a trauma-trained therapist. Imagination, never memory.

modalities.name: Company Before Words
modalities.tagline: Keeping company with inner parts too young to explain themselves.
modalities.whatItIs: Company Before Words is a new, untested approach to parts work for the youngest layers of feeling, the ones that seem to come from before a child could talk. These parts show up as a mood, a pull or a body state with no story attached, so instead of asking them questions, you and a trauma-trained therapist simply keep them company.
modalities.coreIdea: Most parts work runs on questions and answers, but a part formed before language may have nothing to say, and what it may need first is steady company that asks for nothing and aims to change or release nothing. No warmth is produced on purpose: if any comes, it is the plain fact of someone staying.
modalities.whatYouDo: In open, unhurried sessions, the therapist helps you notice a very young-feeling state, such as a heavy, wordless sadness or a startle in the belly, and check that you feel calm and curious toward it. You then stay near it for stretches of several minutes, eyes closed, sometimes with a hand resting where it is felt, while the therapist says very little and now and then asks whether the part seems to notice you there; there are no steps to complete, and the session closes with a few minutes of ordinary talk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People in parts work with a trained therapist who find that some feelings never turn into words or stories, however patiently they ask.
modalities.cautions: Very young feelings can be intense and disorienting, so this belongs only with a therapist trained in trauma care, and anyone with severe dissociation, a current crisis or a tendency to feel spaced out should start there. A wordless state is not a memory and is never treated as evidence of what happened, and the work is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: Some feelings arrive with no story at all, just a heaviness or a startle. Company Before Words is an untested parts-work idea: with a trauma-trained therapist, you keep that very young part company instead of asking it questions. Nothing is dug up.

modalities.name: Interruptions Welcome
modalities.tagline: Treating each distraction in inner work as a part arriving.
modalities.whatItIs: Interruptions Welcome is a new, untested twist on parts work in which nothing counts as a distraction. Every stray thought, itch, plan or sudden urge to joke that breaks in during a session is greeted as a side of you with something to say.
modalities.coreIdea: The moments when attention gets pulled away may be protective sides stepping in at exactly the point where something mattered, so instead of training attention back to one object, every pull is followed and its timing is treated as information.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trauma-trained therapist you begin on a topic that matters to you, and whenever attention is pulled away, by a joke, a plan, an itch or a sudden blank, you pause, name what pulled you and ask that interruption what it wanted you to notice or avoid just then. You follow it for as long as it has something to show, using only memories you already have when a side links itself to the past, while the therapist keeps a written log of when each interruption arrived and what it cut across. At the end you look at the log together and see which sides tend to step in, and at which moments.
modalities.whoItsFor: People in parts work whose sessions keep drifting into jokes, plans or side topics, and who are curious what that drift is doing.
modalities.cautions: Following interruptions can lead quickly toward painful material, so the therapist sets the pace, pauses to ground you if you feel spaced out or unreal, and anyone with dissociation, severe trauma or a current crisis should only try it with a trauma-trained clinician. What surfaces is not evidence of past events, and the work is never used to uncover forgotten memories.
modalities.tweet: In most meditation, a distraction is something to drop. Here each one is treated as a part of you with a message. Interruptions Welcome is an untested parts-work idea, done with a trauma-trained therapist, where every drift gets a hearing.

modalities.name: One Still Frame
modalities.tagline: Holding one remembered moment still and meeting the parts around it.
modalities.whatItIs: One Still Frame is a new, untested approach to parts work done entirely in quiet inner imagery. You take one moment from childhood that you already remember clearly, hold it in mind as a single still picture that never starts to move, and notice which sides of you gather around it, while a trauma-trained therapist sits by, almost silent.
modalities.coreIdea: A memory allowed to play like a film can pull you back inside it, while a single frame held perfectly still may let you stay outside it, calm enough to meet the inner sides that react to it. Stillness is both the safety rail and the method: nothing moves, so nothing has to be relived.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting still with eyes closed, you choose with the therapist a frame that feels manageable, such as standing at the school gate or the back seat on a family car journey, and describe it once in a few words. For the rest of the session you keep it frozen while you notice each side of you that turns up, one that wants to look closer, one that wants to look away, one that feels nothing, and tell the therapist about each in a sentence; if the picture starts to move or feels too close, you shrink it, move it further off or open your eyes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People in parts work who tend to get swept into old memories when they talk about them, and who want a calmer, more contained way to meet the sides that react.
modalities.cautions: Even a still picture can stir strong feeling, so this belongs only with a therapist trained in trauma care, and people with severe trauma, flashbacks or dissociation should choose frames with the therapist's help or not use this at all. Use only moments you already remember; the picture is not evidence of anything beyond what you knew, and it is never used to search for forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: Picture one childhood moment you already remember, frozen like a photo that never starts to play. One Still Frame is an untested parts-work idea: with a trauma-trained therapist, you meet the inner sides that gather around it. Nothing is relived or dug up.

modalities.name: Rated at the Time
modalities.tagline: Comparing how an activity felt then with how you remember it.
modalities.whatItIs: Rated at the Time is a new, untested group format for checking a habit of memory that low mood may encourage: remembering things as worse than they felt while they were happening. Members rate their mood during shared activities, later write down how they think those activities went, and then see how far the memory has drifted from their own ratings.
modalities.coreIdea: Painful conclusions such as 'nothing is ever enjoyable' are often built from memories rather than from the moments themselves, so setting a later memory beside ratings you made at the time gives hard, personal evidence about how the past is being edited. It deliberately adds no warmth or reassurance, only your own data.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to eight people meet weekly for 90 minutes with a trained facilitator, who runs a fixed sequence of three short shared activities, such as a cooperative puzzle, a round of charades and a brisk walk around the building, and every few minutes a timer sounds and each person privately rates their mood from 0 to 10 on a card that is then sealed. At the start of the next session everyone writes how they think each activity went for them, then opens their cards, and the facilitator helps each person compare the two line by line and choose one activity of their own to rate in the moment during the coming week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose low moods come with a sense that nothing is ever good, and who would trust their own numbers more than anyone's reassurance.
modalities.cautions: Seeing low ratings can be discouraging, so the facilitator treats every result as information rather than failure, and anyone with severe depression or thoughts of suicide should be in treatment with a clinician rather than relying on a group concept like this. It is a new idea, not a substitute for established treatment.
modalities.tweet: Low mood can quietly rewrite the past. Rated at the Time is a new, untested group idea: rate your mood during simple shared activities, write a week later how you think they went, then open your sealed cards and compare. Run by a trained facilitator.

modalities.name: Quiz Night for Thoughts
modalities.tagline: Teams race to name the trap in gloomy thoughts.
modalities.whatItIs: Quiz Night for Thoughts is a new, untested group format that turns spotting unhelpful thinking into a fast, noisy team game. Small teams race to name the thinking trap in everyday statements, such as 'they didn't text back, so they're angry with me', and to give a fairer version before the timer runs out.
modalities.coreIdea: Spotting a thinking trap in a calm room is easy, but painful thoughts arrive fast, so practicing at speed, under friendly pressure and with other people calling out answers, may make the skill quicker to reach for in real life. The energy is part of the design: alert, sociable and many items in quick succession rather than one quiet focus.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to twelve people meet weekly for 75 minutes with a trained facilitator, split into teams of three or four standing at tables with a bell. The facilitator reads statements in timed rounds, a team that rings first has 20 seconds to name the trap and offer a fairer version, and in the final round members may volunteer one of their own recent thoughts, read out without any story behind it, for the teams to work on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know the idea of thinking traps but tend to spot them only hours later, and who enjoy games and a bit of noise.
modalities.cautions: Fast games can feel exposing, so nobody has to answer or share a thought of their own, teams are mixed so no one is singled out, and the facilitator stops any laughter aimed at a person rather than a statement. Severe depression, social anxiety or suicidal thoughts call for treatment with a clinician, and this untested idea is not a replacement for it.
modalities.tweet: Picture a pub quiz where every question is a gloomy thought and teams race to name the trap in it. Quiz Night for Thoughts is an untested group idea: fast rounds, a bell, and a fairer version in 20 seconds. Nobody has to share their own.

modalities.name: If-Only Audit
modalities.tagline: Checking whether the other path really led somewhere better.
modalities.whatItIs: If-Only Audit is a new, untested one-to-one method for regrets that run on 'if only I had...'. In sessions led throughout by a trained therapist, you write out the imagined better path step by step and check how likely each step really was, instead of letting the story jump straight to its happy ending.
modalities.coreIdea: An 'if only' story usually skips from the different choice to the best possible outcome, and breaking it into its chain of steps, each given an honest likelihood, may show that the imagined better past was never as certain as it feels. The work stays entirely in thought and on paper, with no movement and no present-moment sensing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each 50-minute session follows the same order: you state one everyday regret in a sentence, such as 'if only I had taken that job', then write the imagined path as numbered steps, from the choice itself to the outcome you picture. The therapist goes through each step with you, asking what else could plausibly have happened at that point, you mark each step as likely, possible or unlikely, and the session ends with a rewritten version of the story that includes the steps it had skipped.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who replay everyday choices, such as a job, a move or a purchase, and keep picturing the better life the other option would have brought.
modalities.cautions: The aim is a fairer picture of the past, not proof that a choice was right, and real losses can still deserve grief. Guilt about serious harm, trauma or a death needs a clinician experienced in that work rather than this untested idea, and persistent rumination with low mood calls for proper treatment.
modalities.tweet: 'If only I'd taken that job.' Regret stories tend to skip straight to the happy ending. If-Only Audit is an untested idea: with a therapist, you write the other path step by step and check how likely each step really was.

modalities.name: Room for Annoyance
modalities.tagline: Cooperating on a shared task while making room for irritation.
modalities.whatItIs: Room for Annoyance is a new, untested group format built on ideas from acceptance and commitment therapy. Small groups work together on a hands-on task and pause now and then to name the irritations and judgments they feel, then carry on cooperating.
modalities.coreIdea: You can feel annoyed with someone and still act on caring about the shared work and the people in it, so aversion is noticed and named in the moment rather than replaced with goodwill.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five or six people meet for two hours with a facilitator and work on a practical task with their hands, such as building a shelf or cooking a meal together. When the facilitator rings a bell, everyone pauses for a minute, notices any annoyance, impatience or judgment, names it in the form 'there's irritation that...' without blaming anyone, and then chooses one helpful action to take as the task goes on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think they must stop being annoyed with others before they can be kind or cooperative, and who would rather practice this with their hands than talk about it.
modalities.cautions: Naming irritation in a group can hurt if it turns into blame, so the facilitator sets firm ground rules, keeps statements about your own reactions and stops any exchange that becomes personal. Tools and cooking come with ordinary safety rules, and this untested idea is no substitute for help with anger or relationship problems that are causing harm.
modalities.tweet: New idea: build or cook something with a small group, and when a bell rings, name the irritation you feel ('there's impatience') without blaming anyone, then pick one helpful next move. Room for Annoyance is an untested take on acceptance skills.

modalities.name: Let Good Moments Go
modalities.tagline: Letting pleasant feelings end as freely as painful ones.
modalities.whatItIs: Let Good Moments Go is a new, untested group practice drawn from acceptance and commitment therapy. It treats clinging to pleasant feelings as the twin of fighting painful ones, and practices letting good moments come and go while you keep doing what matters.
modalities.coreIdea: Grasping at good feelings and trying to repeat them may narrow a life as much as avoiding bad ones, so the willingness usually practiced with pain is practiced here with pleasure: letting a high end on its own.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 75-minute groups with a facilitator, members share one recent moment they tried to hold onto or recreate, such as the glow after praise or the last day of a holiday, and notice together what the grasping felt like and what it cost. In a short exercise each person savors something small, such as a piece of fruit or a favorite song, then notices the wanting for more and chooses whether to act on it, and the session ends with one valued step for the week that does not depend on feeling good.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who chase highs, praise or perfect days and feel flat when they end, and who want a lighter grip on good feelings.
modalities.cautions: Looking at how you chase pleasant feelings can stir low mood or touch on compulsive habits, so anyone with an addiction, an eating disorder or depression should do this with a qualified clinician involved. The savoring exercise never needs to involve food and can use a song or an object instead.
modalities.tweet: We practice letting bad feelings pass. What about good ones? Let Good Moments Go is an untested group idea from acceptance therapy: notice the urge to hold onto a high, let the moment end, and keep doing what matters anyway.

modalities.name: Willingly Bored
modalities.tagline: Staying with a dull but meaningful task while boredom comes along.
modalities.whatItIs: Willingly Bored is a new, untested coaching format that applies acceptance and commitment ideas to boredom. You pick a task that matters to you but feels tedious and practice staying with it, still and unplugged, while boredom does whatever it does.
modalities.coreIdea: Boredom often pushes people away from things they value, such as studying, paperwork or caring for someone, and making room for it, sitting still with no music or distraction, may keep those things within reach.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach trained in acceptance-based methods, you choose one valued but dull task and agree on a block of 15 to 30 minutes with no music, phone or snacks. During the block you keep working, and whenever boredom shows up you silently name how it shows up, such as heavy eyelids or 'this is pointless', then return to the task; in a weekly 30-minute session you look at what boredom said and what got done.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose plans for study, admin or care keep losing out to the urge for something more interesting.
modalities.cautions: Persistent boredom with no interest in anything can be a sign of depression or another condition that deserves a clinician's attention. Take breaks to move and stretch during long blocks, and stop if a task leaves you feeling trapped or very distressed.
modalities.tweet: Boredom quietly cancels a lot of plans. An idea: Willingly Bored has you pick a dull task you actually care about, do it unplugged for 15 to 30 minutes, and simply name what boredom says while you keep going. New and untested, with a coach.

modalities.name: The Room's Best Guess
modalities.tagline: A small group guesses the hidden reason behind your symptom.
modalities.whatItIs: The Room's Best Guess is a new, untested group format for finding the hidden emotional logic behind a symptom. Instead of searching for it alone with a therapist, you describe the symptom to a small, trained group, each member offers one guess at the old expectation that might make it necessary, and you notice which guess lands in your body.
modalities.coreIdea: Other people can often see the sense in a symptom faster than its owner can, and the jolt of recognition when a guess lands may bring an old expectation into awareness more vividly than solitary reflection. The heat and surprise of that moment are part of the method, not a side effect.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five or six people meet weekly for two hours with a therapist trained in this approach and in trauma care, and each week one member describes a recent moment when the symptom took over, such as going blank when praised. Each listener offers one guess in a fixed form, 'maybe part of you expects that if..., then...', about feelings only and never about what happened in the past, and the member says which guess hits hardest, feels it with the therapist's help, puts it in their own words and notices, from memories they already have, how long it has felt true.
modalities.whoItsFor: People puzzled by a reaction they cannot talk themselves out of, who are willing to hear guesses from others in a closely held group.
modalities.cautions: A guess that lands can bring strong feeling, so the group is screened, led by a therapist trained in trauma care, and any member can say 'not that one' without explaining. Guesses are never about past events, nothing said is treated as evidence of what happened, and the work uses only memories you already have and is never used to uncover forgotten ones.
modalities.tweet: What if a few people in a room could see why your symptom makes sense before you can? The Room's Best Guess is an untested group idea: each person offers one 'maybe you expect that if...' guess, and you feel which one lands. Led by a trauma-trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Parent's Own Proof
modalities.tagline: Your own parenting may already contradict what you learned as a child.
modalities.whatItIs: The Parent's Own Proof is a new, untested group format for parents whose childhood lessons flare up while they care for their own children. In a small group led by a specialist therapist, each parent finds the old expectation behind a reaction, then sets it beside the way they actually treat their own child in that same kind of moment.
modalities.coreIdea: A parent who learned 'if you cry, people turn away' may be the very person who picks up a crying child every time, and feeling the old expectation and that lived knowledge together may stop the old lesson feeling like a law about the world. The contradiction is not imagined or borrowed; it comes from what the parent already does.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five or six parents meet every two weeks for two hours with a therapist trained in this approach and in trauma care, and each meeting starts from one member's recent, charged parenting moment, such as freezing when a toddler screamed in a shop. The therapist helps that parent put the old expectation into words and then asks what they did, or would do, for their own child in that moment, and while both are vividly felt the other parents say briefly what they noticed before the group talks it through.
modalities.whoItsFor: Parents and other regular carers of young children who notice their own old fears and freezes flaring up in everyday moments of care.
modalities.cautions: Parenting moments can open old pain quickly, so the group is screened and led by a therapist trained in trauma care, and any parent who feels at risk of harming a child, or is in crisis, needs direct professional help instead. Work only with memories you already have; nothing that surfaces is evidence of past events, and it is never used to uncover forgotten ones.
modalities.tweet: The best evidence against what you learned as a child may be how you treat your own kid. The Parent's Own Proof is an untested group idea: find the old lesson behind a reaction, then set it beside what you actually do. Led by a trauma-trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Well-Thumbed Story
modalities.tagline: A story you loved as a child may already disagree with you.
modalities.whatItIs: The Well-Thumbed Story is a new, untested approach for people who have already found, with a specialist therapist, an old emotional learning behind a symptom. It looks for the contradicting experience in a book, film or tale you returned to again and again as a child, since children often go back to stories that show them something their own lives lacked.
modalities.coreIdea: A story taken in a hundred times in childhood may have been lived from the inside, so a scene in it that breaks your old rule, such as a hero who cries and is comforted, might serve as a vivid, already familiar contradiction. Everything happens in imagination and memory, sitting still, with no movement and no audience.
modalities.whatYouDo: In quiet one-to-one sessions that follow set steps, you name the story and, from what you already remember, retell the scene you returned to most, in the present tense and in as much detail as comes. The therapist then asks you to feel the old learning, such as 'if I need help, I'll be a burden', while you picture that scene vividly, holds the two together with you for a few minutes, and in later sessions checks whether old triggers still bring the same reaction.
modalities.whoItsFor: People in coherence-style therapy who know their old rule but have struggled to find anything that feels like a convincing contradiction, and who loved one particular story as a child.
modalities.cautions: Favorite stories are sometimes tied to painful times, so this is for work with a therapist experienced in trauma care, who helps you choose a story that feels safe and stops if it brings distress. Stay with memories you already have; a story is not evidence about your own past, and the method is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: Many of us reread one story as kids, again and again. The Well-Thumbed Story is an untested idea: with a trauma-trained therapist, you hold an old life lesson beside the scene in that story that quietly disagreed with it. Memory and imagination only.

modalities.name: When the Arms Float
modalities.tagline: Press hard, let go, and let your arms rise on their own.
modalities.whatItIs: When the Arms Float is a new, untested extension of tremor practice that adds a second movement the body makes by itself after effort. After pressing the backs of your wrists hard against a door frame and stepping away, many people find their arms drift upward without trying, and here that float, like the leg tremor, is simply allowed to happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Tremor practice rests on letting an involuntary after-effect of effort run its course, and this goes further into raw, unchosen sensation, with harder effort and more letting be: nothing is pictured, said or wished, and the body's own movements are the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a five-minute warm-up and the usual leg-tiring exercises, you stand in a doorway and press the backs of both wrists outward against the frame, hard but breathing normally, for about 45 seconds, then step forward, let the arms hang and allow them to rise for as long as they rise, two or three times. You finish lying on your back with knees bent for up to ten minutes, letting any leg tremor run and ending it whenever you like by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like tremor practice, or are curious about it, and want more ways to feel the body move without being made to, with no talking or imagery.
modalities.cautions: Hard pressing raises blood pressure, so check with a doctor first if you have heart or blood pressure problems, shoulder or neck injuries, epilepsy or seizures, pregnancy, or recent surgery or fractures, keep breathing throughout, and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Learn tremor practice from a certified provider first, and if moving without deciding to stirs strong emotions, memories or a sense of unreality, stop and get support from a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Press the backs of your wrists hard against a door frame, step away, and your arms may float up by themselves. When the Arms Float is an untested idea that adds this to tremor practice. Doctor check first, keep breathing, stop for chest pain or dizziness.

modalities.name: After the Bounce
modalities.tagline: Bounce on a trampoline, then lie on it and feel the tremor.
modalities.whatItIs: After the Bounce is a new, untested take on tremor practice that tires the legs by bouncing on a large, netted trampoline instead of with set exercises. You then lie on the trampoline bed itself, knees bent, and let the tremor run, feeling each small shake travel through the springy surface beneath you.
modalities.coreIdea: Instead of gathering attention onto one still point, this fills the senses: the lift and drop of bouncing, then a surface that answers every tremor with a faint sway, so attention can spread over the whole body and whatever it touches without being held anywhere. You bounce and rest by feel, not by count.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a few minutes of easy bouncing to warm up, you bounce for 10 to 15 minutes at a pace that makes your legs work and your breath quicken, feet staying low and with no flips or tricks, until the thighs feel tired and shaky. You then lie on your back in the middle of the bed for up to 15 minutes, letting the tremor and the sway it sets off run, end it whenever you like by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side, and sit for a minute before climbing down slowly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know basic tremor practice and find the set exercises dull, or who settle more easily when the body has played first.
modalities.cautions: Trampolines carry a real risk of falls, sprains and neck injury, so use a large netted one with nobody else on the bed, keep jumps low, have another adult nearby, and check with a doctor first if you have heart, joint, bone, balance or pelvic floor problems, epilepsy, pregnancy or recent injuries. Stop for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, learn tremor practice from a certified provider first, and if strong emotions or memories come up, end the round and get a clinician's support.
modalities.tweet: Bounce on a big netted trampoline until your legs are tired, then lie on it and let them shake while the bed sways under you. After the Bounce is an untested take on tremor practice. Low jumps, someone nearby, and a doctor check first.

modalities.name: Stretched Into Shaking
modalities.tagline: Long, cushioned stretches that let a gentle tremor arrive slowly.
modalities.whatItIs: Stretched Into Shaking is a new, untested, entirely solitary version of tremor practice that reaches the tremor through long, supported stretches instead of tiring effort. It follows the same short set of positions every time, at the slowest and quietest pace tremor practice allows.
modalities.coreIdea: Tiring exercises raise effort and breathing before any tremor starts, while a few minutes in each supported stretch may let a mild tremor come with very little exertion, so the whole session can stay settling from start to finish. It is done alone, in silence and in a fixed order, with no music and nobody to move with.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone on a mat with cushions, after two minutes of easy movement to warm up, you hold four set positions for about three minutes each: a reclined butterfly with knees resting on cushions, a low lunge with the back knee down on a pad, lying with legs resting up a wall, and lying on your back with knees bent and feet flat. If a tremor appears you let it run gently, easing out of the stretch a little to soften it, and you finish by lying with legs stretched out for three minutes before rolling onto your side and getting up slowly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want tremor practice without the hard part, such as those who find the standard routine too strenuous or too stirring, and who like a fixed, private routine.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures, pregnancy, hip, knee or back problems, recent surgery, fractures or injuries, or a heart condition, never force a stretch, and stop for pain, chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or panic. Learn tremor practice from a certified provider first, and people with trauma or dissociation should learn this with a clinically trained provider, ending any round by sitting up and looking around the room.
modalities.tweet: What if a tremor could arrive without the hard part first? Stretched Into Shaking is an untested solo idea: hold four cushioned stretches for about three minutes each and let any gentle shake come. Doctor check first, and learn from a certified provider.

modalities.name: Back to Back Sensing
modalities.tagline: Two people sensing inward in silence, backs lightly touching.
modalities.whatItIs: Back to Back Sensing is a new, untested partner practice in the style of Focusing. Two people who know the basic steps sit with their backs lightly touching, each sensing inward in silence, and then share a word or two about what formed.
modalities.coreIdea: Feeling another person breathing at your back, while neither of you asks anything of the other, may make it easier to rest with your own felt sense just as it is: real contact, with no wish or message attached.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a partner agree beforehand on the contact and on a simple way to end it, such as leaning forward, then sit back to back on cushions, fully clothed, for 20 minutes. Each of you lets a felt sense of something in your life form, staying with sensations, the rise and fall of breathing and whatever comes, without trying to change any of it, and afterwards each says one word or image while the other repeats it back without comment.
modalities.whoItsFor: Friends or partners who already practice Focusing and want a quieter, more bodily way to keep each other company.
modalities.cautions: Touch must be fully consensual and easy to stop at any moment, and anyone for whom contact can bring up trauma, or who feels unsure, should skip the contact or work with a qualified therapist. Turning inward can stir strong feelings, so stop if it becomes too much, and anyone in crisis should seek professional help.
modalities.tweet: Two people, backs lightly touching, each sensing inward in silence for 20 minutes, then sharing one word. Back to Back Sensing is an untested idea built on Focusing. Agree on the contact first, and either of you can lean away at any time.

modalities.name: A Friend's Question
modalities.tagline: A friend asks one open question; your body answers first.
modalities.whatItIs: A Friend's Question is a new, untested Focusing-style practice in which someone who knows you well chooses the starting point. They ask one gentle, open question about your life, and you let a bodily felt sense of the answer form before any words come.
modalities.coreIdea: Someone who knows you well may notice what you keep stepping around, so the opening is handed to them, and sensing their question in the body before answering may let something fresh come instead of the usual reply.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a friend who both know the basic Focusing steps meet for about 45 minutes and take turns. The asker offers one open question, such as 'what has been on your mind that you haven't mentioned?' or 'what are you looking forward to?', then stays quiet while the other lets a felt sense form and says words or images only as they come, and the asker reflects back just those words, with no follow-up questions or advice.
modalities.whoItsFor: Close friends or partners who already listen to each other well and want a gentle way to explore what is going on beneath the everyday.
modalities.cautions: Either person can decline a question or stop at any time, and the asker avoids questions about painful history or anything shared in confidence. Anyone with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should explore difficult material with a qualified therapist instead.
modalities.tweet: Let a friend who knows you pick one gentle question, then answer it with your body first: pause, notice what forms, and only then find words. A Friend's Question is an untested idea built on Focusing, and either of you can stop at any time.

modalities.name: Felt but Unsaid
modalities.tagline: Sensing something you have never said, without planning to say it.
modalities.whatItIs: Felt but Unsaid is a new, untested solo practice in the style of Focusing that turns attention to something you have long wanted to say to someone but never have. The aim is not to say it or plan to, only to let a felt sense of carrying it form and be known.
modalities.coreIdea: An unsaid thing carries a bodily feel of its own, and sensing it quietly, with no pressure to express it to anyone, may clarify what it is about. Everything stays inside and still.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone and sitting still for about 20 minutes, after learning basic Focusing from a book or teacher, you bring to mind one unsaid thing, such as a thank-you, a complaint or a question, and notice where and how holding it is felt in the body. You let a word or image come for that sense, check that it fits, and gently ask what it has been like to carry this, then end by writing one line for yourself that you do not send.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry unspoken words toward someone and want to understand them better before deciding anything, or without ever deciding.
modalities.cautions: Unspoken words can be tied to painful relationships or old hurts, so stop if feelings become overwhelming, and anyone with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should do this with a qualified therapist. If the unsaid thing involves harm or danger to you or someone else, talk to a professional or the right service rather than keeping it inside.
modalities.tweet: Nearly everyone carries something they've never said to someone. Felt but Unsaid is an untested idea: sit quietly, notice how carrying it feels in your body, find a word for it, and write one line you don't send. No pressure to say it.

modalities.name: Back on the Old Street
modalities.tagline: Standing, slowly and accompanied, in a place you knew as a child.
modalities.whatItIs: Back on the Old Street is a new, untested idea that takes presence-based work out of the room to a real place from your childhood, such as a street, a park or the outside of a school. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care and one trusted person from your present life, you walk there slowly and let whatever you feel in your body be met, with no plan for what should happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Old emotional learning was formed in real places, through the senses, so meeting it among the actual sights, sounds and smells of one of those places, in the company of people from your life now, may let it be felt more fully than picturing it alone. Nothing is cultivated or wished for: the place is allowed to be what it is, and so are the feelings.
modalities.whatYouDo: After two or three preparation sessions to choose a place you already remember well and can safely visit, agree on stop signals and brief your companion, you spend about 90 minutes there together at walking pace, stopping wherever you are drawn and saying, if you want to, what you feel rather than what you remember. The therapist tracks your body and pace and slows things down, the companion simply stays beside you, and a follow-up session a few days later gives time to settle whatever came up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People doing deep work on their early years who feel that talking about the past in an office keeps it at a distance, and who have a childhood place they can safely visit.
modalities.cautions: Places can bring feelings and memories back with unexpected force, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, never at a place linked to abuse or where someone who harmed you may be, and people with PTSD, dissociation or a current crisis should start with established treatment. Use only memories you already have; nothing that comes up is evidence of past events, and the visit is never used to search for forgotten ones.
modalities.tweet: An untested idea: go back to a street or park from your childhood, slowly, with a trauma-trained therapist and someone you trust, and let the place and your feelings be what they are. It's called Back on the Old Street, and never goes anywhere linked to harm.

modalities.name: Two Pasts, One Room
modalities.tagline: Partners meeting old feelings in each other's quiet company.
modalities.whatItIs: Two Pasts, One Room is a new, untested idea for couples that brings presence-based work on old feelings into the relationship itself. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma and couples work, each partner in turn lets an old feeling be felt in the body while the other stays close, neither fixing it nor explaining it.
modalities.coreIdea: What we learned about closeness as children we learned with other people, so letting it be felt slowly in the company of the person you are close to now, with nothing to solve, may let each partner come to know the other's old ground without it turning into an argument. There are no stages to move through, and nobody is asked to go deeper than they are.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 90-minute sessions with no set agenda, you sit near each other, and whoever feels something stir names it from the inside, such as 'there's an old ache, like being eight and waiting by the window', drawing only on memories you already have, while the therapist slows things down and helps the other partner simply stay, breathing and present. The listening partner may say one sentence about what they feel as they listen, and each session ends with a few quiet minutes and a check that both feel steady enough to go home together.
modalities.whoItsFor: Couples who keep running into each other's old hurts and want to understand them together, slowly, rather than argue about them.
modalities.cautions: This is only for couples without violence, threats or coercion, with a therapist trained in trauma and couples work who first screens each partner alone and can stop any session, and because deep, still states can sometimes bring unreality or fear, people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should start with individual treatment. Use only memories you already have; nothing that comes up is evidence of past events, and it is never used to uncover forgotten ones.
modalities.tweet: Couples often trip over each other's oldest hurts. Two Pasts, One Room is an untested idea: with a trauma-trained couples therapist, one partner slowly feels an old ache while the other just stays close. Never for relationships with violence or coercion.

modalities.name: The Notebook That Stays
modalities.tagline: One notebook for an old feeling, kept safe in the therapy room.
modalities.whatItIs: The Notebook That Stays is a new, untested idea in which a long-carried feeling is given one notebook that never leaves the therapy room. In each quiet session, with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care sitting nearby, you write slowly from the feeling in the present tense, picking up where you left off, and the notebook then stays locked in the therapist's office until next time.
modalities.coreIdea: A feeling carried since early life may need a slow channel and a home of its own outside everyday life, so that it can unfold over months without being acted out, talked over or taken home. Nothing is analyzed or read aloud; the continuity and the safe keeping are the method.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute sessions with no set steps, you sit at a table, let a long-familiar feeling such as 'small and in the way' be there, and write from inside it, for example 'I keep my elbows in', pausing to notice the body whenever the words stop. The therapist says almost nothing, sometimes invites you to slow down or to notice how long this feeling seems to have been with you, and at the end you hand the notebook back, unread unless you choose to show a page.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find old feelings easier to reach on paper than out loud, and who want them met rather than interpreted.
modalities.cautions: Writing from an old feeling can bring up grief or fear, so this belongs with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care who can help you stop and ground yourself, and people with PTSD, severe depression or a current crisis should start with established treatment. Write only from memories you already have; nothing on the page is evidence of past events, and it is never used to uncover forgotten ones.
modalities.tweet: Not writing about an old feeling, but writing as it: 'I keep my elbows in.' The Notebook That Stays is an untested idea: one notebook, written in slowly with a trauma-trained therapist nearby, that never leaves the room. Nothing is analyzed.
